Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> International | National | Politics Asiedu Nketiah urges Africa to turn reparations declarations into practical action 21 November 2026 5:39pm Johnson Asiedu Nketiah, National Chairman, National Democratic Congress (NDC), Ghana Chairman, Bureau Leadership of the African Political Parties Initiative (APPI) Member, Standing Committee of the Movement for Freedom of Nations. ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
National Chairman of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Johnson Asiedu Nketiah, has called on African governments and political leaders to move beyond declarations on reparative justice and pursue practical measures capable of securing redress for historical injustices.
He says Africa has made significant progress in building the institutional framework for reparations but must now give the process greater political support and ensure that commitments translate into enforceable remedies.
Addressing the Movement for Freedom of Nations Assembly in Moscow on November 16, 2026, Mr Asiedu Nketiah said the African Union had established mechanisms to develop a common position on reparations and was working with Caribbean institutions to coordinate legal analysis and diplomacy.
He cited the Accra Reparations Conference of 2023, the African Union's designation of 2025 as the Year of Justice for Africans and People of African Descent Through Reparations, and the Decade of Justice and Reparations for 2026 to 2035 as important milestones.
He also acknowledged the work of the African Union Committee of Experts on Reparations and its Reference Group of Legal Experts in examining the legal, economic, cultural and institutional dimensions of the issue.
Mr Asiedu Nketiah said cooperation between the African Union and the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) was important in building a coordinated campaign, while recognising that the historical experiences and remedies sought by different communities might not be identical.
He commended President John Dramani Mahama, Ghana's leadership in the reparations campaign and his role as the African Union Champion on Reparations.
He also referenced United Nations General Assembly Resolution 80/250, adopted on March 25, 2026, saying the 123 votes in favour represented important international recognition of the gravity of the trafficking and enslavement of Africans.
However, he cautioned that the Movement for Freedom of Nations should complement rather than duplicate the work of established African Union and Caribbean institutions.
He proposed that the Movement could support the process by facilitating access to historical archives, encouraging dialogue with museums and public authorities, and using its relationships with governments and parliaments to advance the work of existing expert bodies.
Mr Asiedu Nketiah said political declarations alone would not secure justice without the legislative, administrative and diplomatic action needed to implement them.
“If legislation prevents the return of cultural property, a parliament must examine it. If an agreement is reached, a government must define and honour its obligations,” he said.
He further insisted that communities affected by historical injustices must have a say in the design of reparative agreements and be able to hold those responsible accountable.
The NDC Chairman also cautioned against presenting ordinary development projects as reparations without demonstrating their connection to the historical wrongs being addressed.
He said apologies, restitution, compensation, access to archives, educational measures and institutional reforms could each address different forms of injustice and should be assessed according to the harm they seek to remedy.
Mr Asiedu Nketiah stressed that the pursuit of reparations should not absolve contemporary African governments of their responsibility to govern effectively, create opportunities and account for public resources.
Equally, he said, failures by present governments should not invalidate legitimate claims arising from historical injustices.
“We have reached a point at which Africa need not merely repeat the case it has made for decades,” he said, urging political leaders to give the existing reparations process practical assistance and ensure that recognition is followed by lasting remedies.
